name: Social skills / game / pickup

card.summary: Pickup 'game' is a commercial seduction-training subculture; some principles have academic support, the community draws strong criticism, and effectiveness claims are untested.
card.note: Some tactics have been widely criticised as manipulative or sexist; the community has been linked to the wider manosphere.

quick.overview:
'Game' is the pickup community's term for skills in meeting and attracting partners, split into inner game (confidence, psychology) and outer game (social skills, fitness, fashion, grooming). It spread through online forums from the 1990s and reached the mainstream with Neil Strauss's 2005 book The Game.

In looksmaxxing, game is often discussed as a complement to appearance. Academic work is limited: one commentator said there was no evidence of effectiveness, while others argued some principles have support in social and evolutionary psychology.
quick.mechanism: Practitioners approach people repeatedly, practise conversation, and follow staged sequences from attraction to comfort to seduction. Some schools use NLP-derived methods, which the scientific consensus treats as pseudoscience.
quick.risks: Critics describe parts of the movement as sexist or misogynistic, and the Southern Poverty Law Center characterises it as male supremacist. Specific tactics such as 'negging' and last-minute-resistance techniques have drawn criticism, and some instructors have faced travel bans after videos of unwanted physical contact.

lead: Social skills, 'game' and pickup refer to learning techniques for meeting and attracting romantic or sexual partners. Practitioners treat attractiveness as more than facial structure: inner game covers confidence and self-esteem, while outer game covers conversation, body language, fitness, fashion and grooming. For looksmaxxers this is the presentation layer, the way an improved appearance gets noticed and turned into a connection, and practitioners believe these skills improve with practice.[1]

Modern pickup writing traces to 1960s and 1970s books, to Ross Jeffries's 'speed seduction' from 1988, and to online forums from 1994. Neil Strauss's 2005 book The Game and the VH1 show The Pick Up Artist (2007 to 2008) brought it to wide attention.[1][2] It has become a commercial market of workshops, books and online coaching.[1]

Looksmaxxing forums have their own social-skills discussion, with long-running series on body language, social psychology and personality, and recurring debate about how much conversation skill matters next to looks.[8][10][9][13] Researchers and commentators disagree about pickup's merits: some say no evidence supports its claims, while others say principles such as generating attraction and building rapport have some support in social and evolutionary psychology.[1] Critics, including the Southern Poverty Law Center, describe the community as sexist or male supremacist.[1]

chain: Practise conversation, body language and approach
An improved appearance is seen and responded to more warmly
angle.text: Practitioners use game to complement grooming, fitness and style: posture, relaxed gestures, eye contact and conversational flow are treated as part of how a person looks and comes across. Forum guides describe calm movement, steady speech and tailoring humour to the other person's interests.

infobox: Ross Jeffries, Erik von Markovik ('Mystery'), Neil Strauss[1][2]

paras: Wikipedia traces the genre to The Art of Erotic Seduction (1967) and How to Pick Up Girls! (1970). Ross Jeffries taught NLP-based seduction from 1988, and the alt.seduction.fast newsgroup started in 1994 and spawned a network of forums and local 'lairs'.[1]

Strauss's The Game chronicled his time in the community, including a bootcamp run by 'Mystery' and the Project Hollywood house. It spent two months on The New York Times bestseller list and drew criticism for misogyny and manipulative tactics.[2] Many forums have since gone offline, and the community now operates largely on Telegram.[1]

Practitioners distinguish day game, night game, message game and social-circle game, and describe approaches ranging from indirect to direct.[1] Named tactics include negging, pawning, 'going caveman' and last-minute-resistance techniques.[1] The Mystery Method (2007) described approaching groups and giving attention to everyone before focusing on a target.[1]

On looksmax.org, social-skills material appears in multi-part guides covering personality types, body language and social psychology.[11][10][9] One guide for younger members advises relaxed posture, slow and controlled speech, small gestures and humour tied to the other person's interests, and describes being observant of cues.[6] Threads such as 'women like guys with good social skills' and 'looks and social skills matter most in scenarios involving new people' argue that conversational ability and looks work together.[12][13] Others argue that looking good is what makes social skills pay off, or that there is little point in improving looks without them.[7][14]
T Nation members have also discussed pickup, including a long thread on 'game' with women in which a poster describes an instructor whose approach rests on confidence and humour.[15]

No studies found testing pickup training as an intervention. Academic work on pickup is descriptive: Hendriks (2012) studied German practitioners and found values combining hedonistic goals with ascetic, disciplinarian ones; a McGill study found men join to address psychosocial deficits while gaining social skills; Oesch and Miklousic (2012) argued several principles have some support in psychology.[1]

Related research on social skills training in other settings includes a 2025 meta-analysis of 17 studies in children with autism that reported small to moderate improvements in social communication, reciprocity and joint attention,[3] and a 2011 meta-analysis of loneliness interventions, in which the most successful randomised studies addressed maladaptive social cognition.[4] A review of social skills training in child psychiatry covers the approach more broadly.[5]

Critics call the movement sexist and misogynistic, and a UCLA centre argued it lies on a continuum of sexist attitudes.[1] In 2014, instructor Julien Blanc was denied entry to the UK and Australia after videos showing him grabbing women.[1] Defenders compared pickup to gym workouts or grooming aids, and Strauss said techniques can be used for good or evil.[1] Strauss concluded in the book that a life devoted only to pickup is unfulfilling.[2]

lore.intro: Looksmax.org members debate whether social skills or looks do more of the work in attracting people, and some write their own guides on conversation and body language.[6][7][8]

claims.claim: Social skills and game are secondary: 'it's all looks'
claims.believers: A thread titled 'Social Skills don't Matter' argues that failed approaches come from appearance, and that once someone ascends it will seem as if their game improved.[7]
claims.experts: Pickup commentators say some principles such as attraction and rapport have support in psychology, while no study has tested pickup training itself.[1]

claims.claim: Social skills and confidence matter alongside looks
claims.believers: Threads such as 'social skills confidence unironically matter' and 'no point in look maxing if you have 0 social skills' argue that appearance without conversational ability falls short.[8][14]
claims.experts: Research on social skills training exists mostly in clinical groups, such as children with autism, where meta-analysis found small to moderate gains in social skills.[3]

claims.claim: Body language and calm delivery can be learned
claims.believers: A guide on looksmax.org recommends slow speech, relaxed posture and small gestures, and the forum has a multi-part series on body language.[6][10]
claims.experts: Practitioners in the pickup community likewise hold that outer game skills improve with practice; academic work on this is descriptive.[1]

claims.claim: Pickup techniques are manipulative and can cause harm
claims.believers: Defenders compare techniques to gym workouts or grooming aids that can be used well or badly.[1]
claims.experts: Critics, including the Southern Poverty Law Center, describe parts of the movement as sexist or male supremacist, and one instructor was denied entry to the UK and Australia in 2014.[1]
